name: Peruvian Causa a la Limeña (Chicken-Filled Potato Terrine)
region: Lima, Peru / Andean and coastal Peruvian foodways
category: Chilled potato terrine with chicken filling
imageAlt: Peruvian causa a la limeña formed into bright yellow potato rounds and garnished with avocado, olive and chile
imageCredit: Photo: F Delventhal, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
summary: Peruvian causa a la limeña layers cool yellow-potato dough seasoned with ají amarillo and lime around a creamy shredded-chicken filling, then finishes it with avocado, egg and olives.
lead: Causa turns potato into architecture: the mash must be dry enough to hold a clean slice yet supple from oil, lime and ají amarillo, with a cool savory filling tucked between two vivid yellow layers.
about: Causa a la limeña is a chilled Peruvian starter built from seasoned yellow potato and a filling that may feature chicken, tuna, seafood or vegetables. Peru's official tourism recipe combines yellow potatoes with ají amarillo, lime and oil, then layers the mixture around chicken and mayonnaise. Avocado, hard-cooked egg, black olives and lettuce are common accompaniments. The potato is not ordinary mashed potato: it is riced while hot, cooled, then worked just enough with the seasoning to become smooth and moldable without turning gluey.
story: Peru Travel presents causa as emblematic of Lima while also recording more than one origin story. Patriotic accounts connect its name to food sold in support of soldiers during either the independence campaign or the War of the Pacific. Other food historians trace causa to the Quechua word kawsay, meaning life or sustenance, and to an older Andean combination of potato and chile. Those explanations need not be forced into a single certainty. The modern dish itself shows layers of history: Andean potato and ají, citrus introduced after European contact, and the composed cold presentation associated with Lima's Creole cooking.
caveat: Causa has many legitimate fillings and shapes; a chicken-filled rectangular terrine is only one Lima-style home presentation. Peruvian papa amarilla gives the best color, flavor and floury texture. Yukon Gold potatoes are the practical North American substitute, but they are moister and less deeply yellow, so steam them dry and add oil cautiously. Bottled ají amarillo paste varies in salt and heat. This recipe uses fully cooked chicken and egg; keep the assembled causa refrigerated and do not leave it at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
prepNotes: Keep water out of the potato
Boil the potatoes whole and unpeeled, then return the riced flesh to the warm pot briefly. Excess water makes a soft causa that slumps when sliced.
Lime juice added to very hot potato can turn bitter, while aggressive mixing can make the starch gummy. Fold the seasoning into potato that is barely warm.
Line the pan for a clean release
A strip of parchment with generous overhang lets the chilled terrine lift out without turning it upside down or crushing the avocado layer.
ingredients: 3 lb Peruvian yellow potatoes or Yukon Gold potatoes, scrubbed
2 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more for the cooking water
3 tbsp ají amarillo paste, plus more to taste
1/3 cup fresh lime juice, divided
1/4 cup neutral oil, plus more only if needed
3 cups cooked shredded chicken breast, about 14 oz
2/3 cup mayonnaise
2 tbsp finely minced red onion
2 tbsp chopped flat-leaf parsley
1/4 tsp freshly ground black pepper
2 ripe but firm avocados
2 hard-cooked eggs, sliced
8 pitted botija or Kalamata olives, halved
Tender lettuce leaves, for serving, optional
steps: Put the whole unpeeled potatoes in a wide pot and cover them with cool water by 1 inch. Salt the water generously, bring to a gentle boil and cook 25 to 35 minutes, depending on size, until a thin knife enters the center without resistance but the skins have not split apart.

Drain the potatoes and let them stand only until safe to handle. Peel while warm and pass them through a potato ricer into the dry pot. Set the pot over low heat for 1 to 2 minutes, folding gently, until visible steam subsides and no moisture films the bottom.

Spread the riced potato on a rimmed tray and cool 20 minutes. Whisk the ají amarillo paste, 1/4 cup lime juice, neutral oil and 1 1/2 teaspoons salt. Drizzle over the barely warm potato and fold with a flexible spatula just until evenly yellow and smooth.

Pinch off a tablespoon of potato mixture and press it between your fingers. It should form a smooth disk without cracking or smearing like wet purée. If crumbly, fold in oil 1 teaspoon at a time; if loose, spread it out and cool completely rather than adding flour.

Mix the shredded chicken, mayonnaise, red onion, parsley, remaining 1 tablespoon lime juice, 1/2 teaspoon salt and black pepper. The filling should hold together on a spoon without pooling mayonnaise; chill it while preparing the pan.

Line an 8-inch square pan with parchment in both directions, leaving overhang. Press half the potato mixture into an even layer about 1/2 inch thick. Use damp fingertips or a second sheet of parchment to level the surface without compacting it hard.

Halve the avocados, remove the pits and peel. Cut the flesh into 1/4-inch slices and arrange it over the potato, leaving a 1/2-inch border. Season with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, then spread the chicken filling gently over the avocado in an even layer.

Flatten the remaining potato mixture between sheets of parchment into an 8-inch square. Peel off the top sheet, invert the potato over the filling and remove the second sheet. Pinch the edges to the bottom layer and smooth the top with a damp offset spatula.
Cover the pan and refrigerate at least 30 minutes and up to 6 hours. Checkpoint: the top should feel cool and firm, and the parchment should pull away from the sides without the potato stretching.

Lift the causa from the pan using the parchment. Wipe a thin knife with a damp towel between cuts and divide into eight rectangles. Each portion should show two distinct yellow potato layers with a neat chicken-and-avocado center.

Serve cold or cool, garnished with egg, olives, lettuce and a small dot of ají amarillo if desired. Refrigerate leftovers promptly in a covered container for up to 2 days; avocado may darken but remains safe when properly chilled.

name: Malaysian Asam Pedas Ikan (Sour-Spicy Fish Stew)
region: Melaka, Malaysia / Malay and Peranakan foodways
imageAlt: Malaysian asam pedas ikan kerisi, fish in a brick-red tamarind and chile broth
imageCredit: Photo: Mdsheth1986, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
summary: Melaka-style Malaysian asam pedas ikan poaches firm fish in a red chile-tamarind broth fragrant with lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, shrimp paste, Vietnamese coriander and okra.
lead: The name is the target—asam for sour and pedas for spicy—with neither sensation hiding the fish, the aromatic paste or the clean grassy note of daun kesum.
about: Asam pedas is a family of sour-spicy stews found across the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and neighboring parts of maritime Southeast Asia. This version is framed around Melaka, where Tourism Malaysia identifies asam pedas as a signature fish dish built on sour tamarind and spices. A pounded chile paste forms the body of the broth; lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and belacan deepen it; tamarind provides the sour center. Firm fish, okra, tomato and daun kesum, also called Vietnamese coriander, cook briefly in the finished gravy so each remains recognizable.
story: Asam pedas cannot be reduced to one national formula. Malay, Minangkabau, Acehnese and Peranakan cooks maintain related preparations with different souring agents, aromatics, fish and names. Melaka's version reflects the port city's long exchange among Malay and Peranakan kitchens, while asam padeh in West Sumatra has its own Minangkabau identity. The Malaysian National Heritage Department lists Melaka's food as a heritage subject, and Tourism Malaysia directs visitors to asam pedas as one of the state's defining tastes. This home recipe follows an established Melakan fish-stew structure without claiming to represent every household or regional branch.
caveat: The chile level in asam pedas is meant to be assertive but is adjustable. Dried chiles differ dramatically in heat, so remove the seeds from some or use a mild long red variety if necessary; reducing chile changes the color and body as well as heat. Belacan contains shrimp and should be omitted for a shellfish allergy, though the broth will lose fermented depth. Daun kesum is characteristic but not always available; cilantro is not an exact substitute. Use firm fish steaks or thick fillets and stop simmering as soon as they turn opaque and flake at the center.
prepNotes: Soak and blend the chiles fully
Softened chile skins should disappear into the paste. A coarse, dry paste scorches before the shallots lose their raw aroma.
Cook the paste until the oil separates
The color should deepen from bright red to brick red and tiny beads of oil should show at the edge before water and tamarind go in.
Okra needs a short head start, but fish can overcook in minutes. Keep the broth below a hard boil after adding it.
ingredients: 8 dried long red chiles, stems removed and seeded in part to taste
1 cup boiling water, for soaking
6 small shallots, peeled and quartered
4 garlic cloves, peeled
1 stalk lemongrass, tender lower third thinly sliced
1 tbsp chopped fresh galangal
1 inch fresh turmeric, peeled, or 1 tsp ground turmeric
1 tsp toasted belacan shrimp paste, optional but traditional
1/3 cup neutral oil
2 additional lemongrass stalks, trimmed and bruised
3 tbsp seedless tamarind concentrate
3 cups water, plus more as needed
1 1/2 tsp palm sugar or light brown sugar
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
8 small okra pods, stem ends trimmed
2 medium tomatoes, cut into wedges
1 small bunch daun kesum or Vietnamese coriander, about 12 leaves
1 1/2 lb firm white fish steaks or thick fillets, such as red snapper, Spanish mackerel or sea bass
Steamed jasmine rice, for serving
steps: Cover the dried chiles with boiling water and soak 20 minutes, until completely pliable. Drain, reserving 1/2 cup soaking liquid, and check for any hard stems or brittle skin.

Blend the softened chiles, shallots, garlic, sliced lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and belacan with 1/4 cup reserved soaking liquid. Scrape the jar repeatedly and add only enough extra liquid to make a smooth, thick paste without visible chile flakes.

Heat the oil in a heavy 4-quart pot over medium-low heat. Add the paste and cook 12 to 18 minutes, stirring and scraping frequently. Checkpoint: the raw onion smell should become sweet and aromatic, the paste should darken to brick red, and small beads of oil should separate around it without any blackened bits.

Add the bruised lemongrass and cook 2 minutes. Whisk the tamarind concentrate with 3 cups water, then pour it into the pot gradually while scraping up the concentrated paste. Add the sugar and 1 teaspoon salt.

Bring the broth to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered 10 minutes. Taste a cooled spoonful: it should be distinctly sour and hot but still savory. Add water 1/4 cup at a time if harshly concentrated, or simmer longer if thin and watery.

Add the okra and simmer 4 minutes. Add the tomato wedges and daun kesum, pressing the leaves into the broth, and simmer 2 minutes more. The okra should be bright green and beginning to tenderize rather than soft.

Pat the fish dry, cut large fillets into four portions and season with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Lower the pieces into the broth in one layer and spoon sauce over the tops. Keep the liquid at a lazy simmer rather than a rolling boil.

Cover partially and cook 5 to 8 minutes, depending on thickness. Checkpoint: the fish should be opaque at the sides, just flake at the thickest point and register 145°F; stop before the pieces split apart into the sauce.

Turn off the heat and rest 5 minutes so the fish finishes gently. Taste the broth again and adjust salt, tamarind or sugar in small increments; the finish should remain sour-spicy, not noticeably sweet.

Discard the large lemongrass stalks. Serve the fish, okra, tomato and plenty of broth with steamed rice. Cool leftovers within 2 hours and refrigerate up to 2 days; reheat the broth gently and add the fish only long enough to become hot so it does not toughen.

name: Egyptian Koshary (Rice, Lentils, Pasta and Chickpeas)
type: Layered Rice, Lentil and Pasta Bowl / Main
category: Rice, lentil, pasta and chickpea main
imageAlt: Egyptian koshary topped with chickpeas, crisp fried onions and bright tomato sauce beside garlic-vinegar and chile sauces
imageCredit: Photo: Dina Said, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
summary: Egyptian koshary layers cumin-scented rice and brown lentils with pasta and chickpeas, then adds concentrated tomato sauce, sharp garlic-vinegar daqqa and a crown of crisp onions.
lead: Koshary is abundance assembled from pantry staples: each grain and pulse keeps its texture, while tomato sauce, daqqa, chile and fried onions let every diner tune the same generous bowl.
about: Koshary is an Egyptian everyday dish made from inexpensive staples cooked separately and assembled in layers. UNESCO's description centers rice, pasta, black lentils and fried onions, with vinegar, garlic and hot sauce added according to preference; chickpeas and tomato sauce are also central to the widely recognized modern bowl. Good koshary is not a soft mixed casserole. The rice is fluffy, the lentils tender but intact, the pasta chewy, the chickpeas creamy, the tomato sauce concentrated, and the onions emphatically crisp. Daqqa, a sharp garlic-vinegar condiment, wakes up all of those starches at the table.
story: UNESCO inscribed the daily-life dish and practices associated with koshary on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2025, emphasizing its affordability, broad social reach, street and restaurant culture, and role in sharing and community. The Smithsonian's account cautions against a single neat origin story. A mid-19th-century written reference describes a rice-lentil-onion dish in Suez, while pasta, chickpeas and the modern sauces accumulated over time. Connections to Indian khichdi, Mediterranean migration and older Egyptian grain-and-legume eating are discussed, but the exact path remains debated. Today's layered bowl is unmistakably part of Egyptian daily life.
caveat: Spellings include koshary, koshari and kushari. Component ratios, pasta shapes, lentil varieties and sauce heat differ among vendors, regions and homes. This version uses brown lentils and medium-grain rice cooked together after the lentils receive a head start; separate cooking is equally valid and gives even more control. Canned chickpeas make the home workflow manageable. Fry onions cautiously in a stable neutral oil, keep children away from the hot pan, and let the onions darken only to deep golden because they continue crisping after removal.
prepNotes: A mandoline makes consistent 1/8-inch slices, but use its hand guard. Uneven onions burn before thicker pieces crisp.
Start the onions and tomato sauce first, then the lentils and rice, and boil the pasta last. Koshary is best when all components are warm and distinct at assembly.
Serve tomato sauce, garlic-vinegar daqqa and chile sauce individually so diners can build the acidity and heat they prefer.
ingredients: 3 large yellow onions, sliced into even 1/8-inch half-moons
3/4 cup all-purpose flour
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
2 cups neutral oil, for frying
1 cup brown or black lentils, rinsed and picked over
1 cup medium-grain white rice, rinsed until the water is nearly clear
1/2 cup broken vermicelli noodles
1 tsp ground cumin, divided
4 cups water, divided, plus more for pasta
8 oz small elbow macaroni or ditalini
1 can chickpeas, 15 oz, drained and rinsed
5 garlic cloves, finely minced, divided
2 tbsp tomato paste
1 can crushed tomatoes, 28 oz
1 tsp ground coriander
1/2 tsp red chile flakes, plus more to taste
1/2 cup white vinegar, divided
2 tbsp fresh lemon juice
1 small hot chile, minced, optional
steps: Toss the sliced onions with the flour and 1/2 teaspoon salt, separating every strand. Heat 1 inch of oil in a wide heavy skillet to 325°F. Shake excess flour from half the onions and fry 8 to 12 minutes, stirring often, until evenly deep golden. Transfer to a rack or paper towels, then repeat with the remaining onions.

Let the onions cool uncovered. Checkpoint: they may feel slightly flexible when first lifted but should become crisp within 5 minutes. If still leathery, return them to 325°F oil for 1 to 2 minutes; discard any bitter black pieces. Reserve 3 tablespoons onion oil for cooking.

Put the lentils and 2 cups water in a medium saucepan. Bring to a boil, reduce to a simmer and cook 12 minutes. The lentils should be partly tender but still firm at the center; drain only if more than 1/2 cup liquid remains.

Heat 1 tablespoon reserved onion oil in a separate heavy saucepan. Toast the vermicelli over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes until nut-brown. Stir in the rice, lentils, 1/2 teaspoon cumin, 1/2 teaspoon salt and 2 cups water. Bring to a boil, cover, reduce to low and cook 15 minutes.

Remove the rice-lentil pot from the heat and rest, covered, 10 minutes. Fluff gently with a fork. The rice should be separate and the lentils tender but intact; if either is still firm, sprinkle in 2 tablespoons hot water, cover and steam over the lowest heat for 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 2 tablespoons reserved onion oil in a saucepan over medium. Cook 3 minced garlic cloves for 30 seconds, then stir in the tomato paste, coriander, remaining 1/2 teaspoon cumin and chile flakes for 1 minute. Add the crushed tomatoes and 1/2 teaspoon salt.

Simmer the tomato sauce uncovered for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until brick red and thick enough that a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a path for a second. Stir in 2 tablespoons vinegar, taste and adjust salt or chile.

For the daqqa, crush the remaining 2 garlic cloves with a pinch of salt. Whisk with 1/4 cup vinegar, lemon juice and 1/4 cup water. For optional shatta, mix the minced hot chile with the remaining 2 tablespoons vinegar and 2 tablespoons tomato sauce; set both condiments aside.

Boil the macaroni in well-salted water until just al dente according to the package. Drain thoroughly. Warm the chickpeas in a small saucepan with 1/4 cup water and a pinch of salt for 5 minutes, then drain.

To assemble each bowl, spoon in rice and lentils, add a layer of macaroni and scatter over chickpeas. Ladle on tomato sauce and crown with a generous handful of crisp onions. Serve daqqa and shatta at the table rather than stirring them into the full batch.

Eat immediately while the onions are crisp and the components are warm. Store onions airtight at room temperature for 1 day and refrigerate all other components separately for up to 4 days; reheat the rice, lentils, pasta and sauce to steaming before assembling.
